title: Comparative analysis of the MINSA Health Map and the Harmonized Health Facility Assessment
text:
Opening
Angola has two instruments that look at its health facilities. The Health Map, produced by the Office of Studies, Planning and Statistics, is a national registry with four editions and full country coverage: it knows which facilities exist, where they are, what type they are and which services they report offering. The Harmonized Health Facility Assessment (HHFA), from the World Health Organization, is a standardized survey of 2,604 indicators that measures, beyond the existence of a service, what the facility has in place to deliver it — guidelines, trained staff, equipment, diagnostics and medicines. This book is the result of a comparison between the two, carried out item by item, with a practical aim: to identify what the HHFA can add to the Health Map without altering its character, and what the Health Map brings that no international instrument can.
The comparison rests on an inversion of logic that runs through the whole work. The HHFA is not organized around questions but around indicators — the questions exist because an indicator needs them. Applied to the Health Map, that logic reveals that many HHFA indicators are already latent in the Registration Form: the question is there, the topic is there, and what is missing are the response options that allow the calculation. A second finding made the path shorter than expected — the HHFA inventory sets aside two entire subareas, 1.3.2 and 1.3.3, for instruments that measure availability without applying the readiness module. That is precisely the Health Map’s case. By that route, a revised Form comes to produce 345 HHFA indicators, with nineteen complete subareas, and more than nine in ten requiring no field observation.
The chapters follow the order in which the work was done. Chapter 1 gives the overview: the pattern of each instrument and where one adds to the other. Chapter 2 deals with question design, showing how vague wording loses information the definition already contained. Chapter 3 maps coverage item by item, with eight comparison categories and an interpretive comment after each block. Chapter 4 proposes thirty concrete increments to the Form, each with the indicator it produces, its cost, the collection mode it requires and what is gained for public health. These are followed by Decisions we will need to take to move forward together, with the working agenda and the calendar to December; the revised Form, with every question written out in full and the indicator annotated on each; and Annex 1, the clean questionnaire, ready to be discussed in a meeting.

title: 1  Overview
text:
⚠ READ THIS FIRST: the scope of this analysis
This is the first of three documents. It gives the overview: what each instrument asks, and where one adds to the other.
We are now comparing questions with questions. The earlier analysis used the information published in the 2024 Luanda report. This one is based on the data collection form and its filling guide, which is where one sees what was actually asked, of whom, and against what criterion.
One caveat for the reader: the form is an annual registration form for facilities of the National Health Service and has a purpose of its own, which is not the HHFA's. The differences noted here are not shortcomings; they are opportunities to add information where it is cheap to collect.

title: 1  Overview
section: The pattern of the Health Map
text:
The pattern of the Health Map
The form has 12 sections and about 108 service boxes, and always answers the same question: does the service exist and is it working? Yes or no.
The collection rule is set out in the guide: information is obtained through an interview with the facility manager or deputy, and by consulting the facility’s statistics and other documents (guide, sheet 3).
An important note on verification. In practice, Health Map data collection happens in two steps: the manager reports, and the team then verifies on site. This was told to us by the Health Map management and does not appear in the form or in the guide. Verification therefore happens in the field but is not recorded: a ticked box does not distinguish what was confirmed from what was only reported, and that distinction is lost in the database and in the report.
There are three exceptions, where the form goes beyond yes or no:

Bed resources: counts observation beds, inpatient beds, delivery tables, dental chairs and cots.
Medical and surgical devices (health centres and health posts only): counts 15 device types usually in working order.
Means of transport: counts working and non-working vehicles separately.

The HHFA starts from the same question and adds three layers:

Verification: it distinguishes what the enumerator observed from what was reported.
Readiness: guidelines, trained staff, equipment, diagnostics and medicines for each service.
Continuity: supply stock-outs in the past three months.

The HHFA prepares the ground and allows us to move to the next stage, which is to obtain evidence on how many people are seen and with what result.

title: 1  Overview
section: What the Health Map form captures and the HHFA does not
text:
What the Health Map form captures and the HHFA does not
This is the adaptation material the HHFA requires from each country and does not bring with it.

Identity and distance of the referral facility (3.2): category, name, distance in minutes, total kilometres, paved kilometres and dirt-track kilometres. The HHFA asks whether a referral mechanism, protocols, records and feedback exist (Q1227 to Q1231), but does not record where patients are referred to, or how far.
Building floor area in square metres, number of buildings and staff residences (4.1 to 4.4).
Year, period and construction material (4.5 to 4.7).
Physical condition of the building in one of four intervention categories, with criteria detailed by building element in the guide — foundations, structure, floor, walls, roof, false ceiling and latrine (5.1, guide, sheet 8) — and the square metres in each condition, which allow the works to be costed. The HHFA records defects room by room, but issues no such judgement and measures no areas.
Wastewater treatment plant, and whether it works (6.7). The HHFA touches the subject only through maintenance of the sanitation system.
Fleet inventory by type, working and non-working (10.1).
Teaching role of the facility (7.4.8 and 7.4.9): health technical training school and continuing education unit, with placement fields for medicine and for nursing.
Number of mortuary drawers (7.5.5).


A confusion that is easy to make. Several topics that look exclusive to the form are in fact in the HHFA, but in module 4 (management and finance) and among the additional questions, not the core ones:

catchment population: 4.5.2.6.1 to 4.5.2.6.9 — defined catchment area, population estimate, source of the estimate, number of pregnant women, infants and children under 5, and list of registered patients;
kitchen, laundry and cleaning, building maintenance, human resources, social services and general administration: 4.1.1.2.1 to 4.1.1.2.8;
mortuary: 4.1.1.2.7;
management bodies: 4.1.1.1.1 to 4.1.1.1.4 (governing board met in the past 6 months, management committee in the past 3, finance committee, community member on the board) and 4.1.1.3.1 (procurement committee);
vehicles: 2.7.1.1.6 (vehicle and driver available 24 hours) and 4.1.2.3.1 and 4.1.2.3.2 (maintenance schedule and adherence to it);
secondary sources of water and energy: 2.1.1.2.4 and the questions on interruptions in the past 7 days.

In an application using only the core availability and readiness questionnaires, none of this is collected. It is a design decision, not a property of the instrument.

title: 1  Overview
section: What the HHFA adds within the same domains
text:
What the HHFA adds within the same domains
1. Verification is recorded in the answer. Where the form has a yes/no box, the HHFA has three responses: observed; reported, not seen; not available. The instruction to the enumerator sits in the question itself (“if yes, ask to see it”). The verification the Health Map team already performs in the field would then live in the data, not only in the memory of whoever collected it.
2. Availability and functionality are two questions. For each equipment item the HHFA first asks (A) whether it is available, with the three options above, and then (B) whether it works. The form already uses this logic for vehicles, separating working from non-working.
3. Readiness, organized in four domains. For each service the facility reports offering, the HHFA checks:

staff and guidelines: national or other guidelines available on site, and staff trained in the past 2 years;
equipment: the devices that service requires;
diagnostics: the tests required, distinguishing what is done on site from what is sent out with results returned;
medicines and commodities: the tracer items for that service, observed and within their expiry date.

For diabetes this is 12 items; for tuberculosis and antenatal care, more than 20 each.
4. Service components, one by one. The Health Map guide already defines several services precisely. The HHFA turns those definitions into separate questions:

antenatal care: the guide defines complete antenatal care through a list (card, history, weight, oedema, fundal height, mucosa, blood pressure, Leopold manoeuvres, intermittent preventive treatment for malaria, iron and folic acid, deworming, counselling) and the form settles it in one box; the HHFA asks item by item;
delivery: where the form has basic and comprehensive emergency obstetric care, the HHFA asks about the signal functions one by one (parenteral antibiotic, oxytocic, anticonvulsant, manual removal of placenta, removal of retained products, assisted vaginal delivery, neonatal resuscitation);
sterilization: the HHFA asks which equipment is present (electric autoclave, dry heat sterilizer, non-electric autoclave, heat source), whether it works, and where the central reprocessing site is.

5. Disaggregation of provision. By age group (under 5, 5–14, adolescents and adults) and by function within the service: diagnose, treat, counsel, refer and follow up. The form records the service as a whole.
6. Continuity of supply. Stock-outs of tracer items in the past 3 months, and stock-outs by vaccine in the immunization programme. This separates a one-off gap from a structural supply failure.
7. An explicit reference period. Every question states its moment: today, past 7 days, past 3 months, past 2 years. On the form, “in working order” fixes no period.
8. Where to look for the item. The HHFA tells the enumerator which room to check (service site, laboratory, pharmacy, store) and, for several items, accepts presence anywhere in the facility. The form does not specify the place of verification.
9. Explicit denominator. The HHFA separates what is computed over all facilities (provision) from what is computed only over facilities offering the service (readiness). This prevents comparing percentages with different bases.

title: 1  Overview
section: Conclusion: what the HHFA can bring to the Health Map form
text:
Conclusion: what the HHFA can bring to the Health Map form
The two instruments do not compete, and neither replaces the other. The HHFA is standardized and international, which allows Angola to be compared with itself over time and with other countries. But it does not work without country adaptation: its own rules state that data collection is driven by the indicators the country needs, and that lists and categories flagged for adaptation — facility types, staff categories, essential medicines, national guidelines — must be replaced with national ones. The Health Map form and its guide are the source of that material.
In the other direction, the form can gain precision through short additions, without changing its logic or greatly lengthening the visit:

Record the verification that already happens. Collection already combines the manager’s report with on-site checking. It is enough for the box to carry three responses — observed; reported, not seen; not available — for that verification to live in the data.
Check functionality on the day of the visit for devices, as the form already does for vehicles.
Add three readiness questions to the services already listed: guidelines available, staff trained in the past two years, and tracer medicine in stock.
Record stock-outs of tracer items in the past three months.
Split into separate boxes the definitions the guide already carries, for example complete and incomplete antenatal care, which today share a single box.
State the reference period in each question.

These are direct-observation additions, feasible within the same visit and by the same team, which make the Health Map more specific and more precise for what it already sets out to do: support decisions about the health facility network.

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
text:
⚠ READ THIS FIRST
This is the second of three documents. The first gave the overview. This one deals with the design and presentation of questions. The third will map coverage, item by item.
One finding runs through the whole document: the Filling Guide is, at several points, as precise as the HHFA. It defines what counts as complete antenatal care, what a minimum laboratory is, what sterilization by a reliable method means, and what a bed is. The precision is in the guide; what is lost is its recording on the Health Map Form, because the available answer is a single box.
For that reason, almost none of the adjustments proposed here call for new questions. They call for the Health Map Form to record what the guide already instructs the team to check.

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: The principle: the question decides the data
text:
The principle: the question decides the data
Every survey question decides three things at once:

Who answers, and with what knowledge.
What counts as “yes” — the criterion.
Which moment the answer refers to.

When any of the three is left implicit, it is the enumerator who decides, alone, at the door of the room, with the respondent waiting. And because the decision is not recorded, no one can later tell what it was.
The test used throughout this document is always the same: faced with an in-between situation, what does the enumerator tick? If the form does not answer that, the answer varies from team to team, and that variation enters the results without leaving a trace.

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: 1. Who answers, and in which room
text:
1. Who answers, and in which room
On the Health Map Form. The guide states that information is obtained “through an interview with the facility manager or deputy, and by consulting the facility’s statistics and other documents” (sheet 3). The same respondent answers for every section, from the laboratory to the hospital committees, and the form does not say where each question should be asked.
In the HHFA. Each block opens with a routing instruction, written in capitals for the enumerator:

“ASK TO BE SHOWN THE LOCATION IN THE FACILITY WHERE NONCOMMUNICABLE DISEASE SERVICES ARE PROVIDED. FIND THE PERSON MOST KNOWLEDGEABLE ABOUT NCD SERVICES IN THE FACILITY. INTRODUCE YOURSELF, EXPLAIN THE PURPOSE OF THE SURVEY AND ASK THE FOLLOWING QUESTIONS.” (i1502)

Laboratory, pharmacy, maternity and emergency each have their own respondent and their own place of verification.
The enumerator’s dilemma. The director is asked whether urine ketone strips are available. The director does not work in the laboratory. If they answer in good faith “yes, we have them”, the answer describes what is usually there. Nobody opened the drawer.
Effect on measurement. The bias is predictable and has a direction: answers obtained away from the place tend to describe the normal situation and to overstate availability on the day.
Adjustment. One instruction line per section, saying where to go and whom to speak to. No new questions.

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: 2. The verification that is done but not recorded
text:
2. The verification that is done but not recorded
On the Health Map Form. Collection already happens in two steps: the manager reports and the team verifies on site. That verification has nowhere to be recorded, because the box is yes or no.
In the HHFA. The verification instruction sits inside the question, and its result sits inside the answer:

“Are national guidelines for the diagnosis and/or management of diabetes available in this service site today? If yes, ask: May I see the guidelines?”
Responses: 1 yes, observed · 2 yes, reported, not seen · 3 no (Q1507)

The enumerator’s dilemma. The manager says the guidelines exist, but they are locked in a cupboard and the key is with the head nurse, who is not in today. With two options, the enumerator must choose between “yes”, which erases the doubt, and “no”, which is unfair to the facility. Almost everyone chooses “yes”.
Effect on measurement. Two situations — guideline seen and guideline reported — count as one. The bias is upward and systematic, because the enumerator always errs on the same side.
Adjustment. Three responses for items that can be seen. Collection time does not change: the question is already asked; only the answer gains a cell.

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: 3. The moment the answer refers to
text:
3. The moment the answer refers to
On the Health Map Form. The expressions used are “in working order”, “exists and is currently working” (guide, sheets 10, 12, 14 and 15) and, in section 9, “medical and surgical devices usually in working order”.
In the HHFA. Each question fixes its moment, and the moment changes with what is being asked:







Question
Moment




“Is the incinerator functional today?” and “is fuel available today?” (Q1219, Q1220)
today


“During the past 7 days, was electricity available, from the main or any backup source, at all times the facility was open for services?” (Q1209)
past 7 days


“At any time during the past 3 months has oxygen been unavailable for this service site for any reason?” (Q2653)
past 3 months


“Have you or any provider of diabetes services received any training in the diagnosis and/or management of diabetes in the past 2 years?” (Q1509)
past 2 years



The enumerator’s dilemma. The ultrasound machine broke three weeks ago and the part has been ordered. “Usually in working order” says yes. “Working today” says no. Both answers are right, each for its own question, but the form does not say which question is being asked.
Effect on measurement. With no period fixed, each team resolves it differently and the provincial result mixes installed capacity with actual availability. Since “usually” is the more generous reading, the bias is upward.
Adjustment. Write the period into each question. Where installed capacity is what matters, say “usually”; where the real situation is what matters, say “today”.

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: 4. Composite concepts in a single box: where specificity is lost
text:
4. Composite concepts in a single box: where specificity is lost
This is the point of greatest information loss, and also the one where the Filling Guide is richer than the Health Map Form can record.

4.1 Laboratory
What the guide says (sheet 12). Laboratory: “at a minimum, thick smear, haemoglobin or haematocrit, and simple stool and urine tests”.
What the form offers. One box: 7.2.1 Laboratory, tick if it exists.
The real situation, which is the most common one. The facility does thick smears and haemoglobin. It does not do stool or urine tests, because there are no strips. What gets ticked?

If the enumerator ticks yes, the facility enters the report alongside a complete laboratory.
If they tick no, a facility that diagnoses malaria and anaemia every day disappears from the map.

Neither answer is true, and the form forces a choice. In practice the tendency is to tick “yes”, because the service does exist and the enumerator does not want to penalize the facility.
How the HHFA solves it. It does not ask whether there is a laboratory. It asks, test by test, whether it is done on site, whether the sample is sent out with results returned, or whether it is not done. It then asks about the corresponding equipment and reagents:

“I would like to know if the following tests are available in this service site today. For each test, please show it to me.”
Responses per item: 1 at least one not expired · 2 available but expired · 3 reported available, not seen · 4 not available today · 5 never available (Q2911)

What is gained. The same facility now appears as “does malaria and haemoglobin, does not do urine or stool”. That is a sentence one can act on when deciding what to buy.


4.2 Antenatal care
What the guide says (sheet 12). It instructs the team to record whether the consultation is “complete, incomplete or not provided”, and defines the complete one through a list: pregnancy card, history, weight, oedema, fundal height, mucosa, blood pressure and Leopold manoeuvres, plus intermittent preventive treatment for malaria, immunization, iron and folic acid, deworming and counselling.
What the form offers. One box: 7.3.6 Antenatal care.
The real situation. The facility weighs, measures blood pressure and gives iron, but has no blood pressure device in three of its four consulting rooms, does not test for syphilis, and has had no sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine for two months. What gets ticked? “Yes” — and the report will say that 96% of facilities offer antenatal care, the same figure they would have if every one of them provided the complete consultation.
How the HHFA solves it. Provision is broken down by component and readiness is checked item by item: HIV and syphilis testing in pregnancy, haemoglobin, urine test, iron and folic acid, tetanus vaccine, intermittent preventive treatment for malaria, each with its own answer.
What is gained. There is no longer a need to choose between “has” and “does not have”. The facility is described by what it does and by what it lacks.


4.3 Delivery: basic emergency obstetric care
What the form offers. Two boxes: 7.3.7.1 basic and 7.3.7.2 comprehensive emergency obstetric care. The guide defines the basic one as parenteral antibiotic, oxytocin and anticonvulsant, manual removal of the placenta and removal of retained products.
The real situation. The facility does all of that except the anticonvulsant, because there is no magnesium sulfate. What gets ticked? The definition is a set: one element missing means it is not basic emergency obstetric care. But ticking “no” makes this facility equal to one that performs none of the five functions.
How the HHFA solves it. It asks about the seven signal functions one by one, and additionally checks whether the corresponding medicine is on site and within its expiry date.
What is gained. One knows exactly which function is missing, and whether it is missing for lack of a medicine, of equipment or of training. A facility missing only magnesium sulfate is a procurement problem; a facility missing everything is a network design problem.


4.4 Minor surgery
What the guide says (sheet 10). “Minor surgery (dressings): treatment of wounds and injuries, dressings and injections.”
The specificity problem. The definition places the simple dressing, which any health post does, alongside suturing and abscess drainage, which require sterile supplies, local anaesthetic and trained staff. With this wording almost every facility ticks “yes”, and the box stops distinguishing anything.
How the HHFA solves it. It lists the procedures: suturing of laceration, incision and drainage of abscesses, wound debridement, acute burn management, chest tube insertion, removal of a foreign body. And it checks the supplies: minor surgical kit, sterile gloves, skin disinfectant, lidocaine, sutures.


4.5 The general rule these four cases point to
A single box works well only when the concept is indivisible. When the concept is a list — and in these four cases it is — the single box forces the enumerator to round, and rounding is almost always upward. What is lost is not decimal precision: it is the ability to say what is missing. And that is exactly what an investment plan needs to know.

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: 5. Existing and functioning are not the same
text:
5. Existing and functioning are not the same
On the Health Map Form. For the committees in section 7.4 — ethics, hospital infections, deaths, medicines, occupational safety, discipline and audit — the guide says only “indicate whether it exists”. For the continuing education unit, it already adds a time criterion: “that has been operating in the past 6 months” (sheet 14).
In the HHFA. The criterion is always functioning: governing board that met in the past 6 months (4.1.1.1.1), management committee that met in the past 3 (4.1.1.1.2), finance committee (4.1.1.1.3), and how often the committee refers to the management plan in its decisions (Q509).
The enumerator’s dilemma. The infection committee was created by decree in 2019 and has never met. Does it exist? On paper, it does.
Effect on measurement. What is measured is formality rather than practice, and the result does not distinguish a facility that manages hospital infection from one that has merely appointed a committee.
Adjustment. Extend to the committees the criterion the guide already applies to the continuing education unit.
crumbs: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
text:
6. Regular and irregular services
On the Health Map Form. The guide is explicit: “services offered on an irregular basis must be duly identified” (sheet 10). And it gives the rule: a service provided only when the doctor is on the rota is irregular, but “shall be considered regular if the doctor can be called in even when not present at the facility”.
The problem. The form has no field to flag irregularity, so the instruction cannot be carried out. And the on-call rule is generous: it is enough that someone can be called for the service to count as regular.
In the HHFA. Time availability is measured by its own questions: hours per day the facility is open (Q1302), days per week (Q1304) and, in emergency care, two distinct questions — a dedicated 24-hour emergency unit (3.5.1.1.2) and medical and nursing staff on site 24 hours (3.5.1.1.3).
The enumerator’s dilemma. The health post sees patients until 3 p.m. and, at night, a nurse who lives next door is called when needed. By the rule, that is a regular emergency service. On the form it looks the same as a centre with a team on site 24 hours.
Adjustment. A frequency column for the services where it changes the reading: daily, weekly, monthly, on call.
crumbs: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: 7. Zero, don’t know and not answered
text:
7. Zero, don’t know and not answered
On the Health Map Form. Catchment population is filled in “if known” (guide, sheet 6); the year of construction is “not compulsory”; there is no “don’t know” option in the service boxes.
In the HHFA. “Don’t know” is a coded option in about 70 questions, mostly on equipment functionality, and unknown values have their own code, distinct from zero.
The enumerator’s dilemma. Asked how many inpatient beds there are, the manager is not sure and the ward is locked. Leave it blank, or write an approximate number?
Effect on measurement. An empty field may mean absence, ignorance or an oversight. In analysis, empty tends to be read as absent, and items with many blanks come out low. Worse, the three cases become indistinguishable after collection.
Adjustment. Add “don’t know” where the answer depends on memory, and use a distinct code for not answered.
crumbs: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: 8. What is left in free text
text:
8. What is left in free text
On the Health Map Form. The square metres by condition — the figure that allows the works to be costed — are recorded in the observations field of section 5. The bed, device and transport sections have free lines for adding unlisted items.
In the HHFA. Quantities have their own numeric fields and lists are closed, with national adaptation done before fieldwork rather than during it.
Effect on measurement. Free text cannot be tabulated without later coding, and items added by each team are hard to compare across municipalities. The data exist, but do not reach the table.
Adjustment. Four numeric fields for the square metres by condition. Closed lists, reviewed at each edition.
crumbs: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
section: 9. Long lists without a gate question
text:
9. Long lists without a gate question
On the Health Map Form. Section 7.1 has 36 boxes for clinical and surgical specialties, ticked in sequence. In a health post, 33 of them are “no”.
In the HHFA. There is a gate question per block, with a skip: if the facility offers no noncommunicable disease services, all questions on diabetes, hypertension and respiratory disease are skipped (Q1500). This is what allows the instrument to be long without every facility answering everything.
Effect on measurement. Long lists where almost everything is “no” tire both respondent and recorder. Error concentrates in the last lines, and it is always the same kind of error: leaving unticked something that exists.
Adjustment. Gate questions per block, with clearly signposted skips. On an electronic device the skip is automatic.
crumbs: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options

title: 2  A note on the design and presentation of questions and response options
text:
10. Counting devices or measuring availability
On the Health Map Form. Section 9 counts the number of devices of each type, for health centres and health posts. The report presents provincial totals, for example 323 adult scales.
In the HHFA. The indicator is the percentage of facilities with the item available and functional.
Effect on measurement. The provincial total does not say how many facilities have at least one scale: one facility with five offsets five with none. For logistics the total is useful; for deciding where to invest, distribution is what counts.
Adjustment. Keep the count and add to the report the percentage of facilities with at least one item available and functional. This is a change in analysis, not in collection.

title: 3  What each instrument captures about the reality of health facilities
text:
The five dimensions of the HHFA
The HHFA organizes everything it collects into five service dimensions. It is worth having them in mind before going into the tables, because the comparison with the Health Map Form changes in nature from one dimension to the next.
1. General service availability — 428 indicators
What the facility is: infrastructure, beds, workforce and the services it reports offering. This is the dimension closest to the purpose of the Health Map Form, and where the overlap between the two instruments is greatest.
2. General service readiness — 225 indicators
What the facility has in place, whatever services it offers: water, energy, sanitation, amenities, basic equipment, diagnostic capacity, essential medicines, consumables, storage, infection prevention, referral and emergency preparedness. Almost all of it is observed by the enumerator.
3. Service-specific availability and readiness — 1,484 indicators, 57% of the total
Service by service — family planning, antenatal care, delivery, child health, immunization, malaria, tuberculosis, HIV, noncommunicable diseases, surgery, emergency care, laboratory — what the facility offers and what it has to deliver it: guidelines, trained staff, equipment, tests and medicines. This is the HHFA’s dominant dimension and the one with least overlap with the Form.
4. Management and finance — 358 indicators
How the facility is run: governance, budget, funding sources, maintenance, staff support, information systems and quality systems.
5. Clinical quality of care — 109 indicators
What was done for the patient, through review of clinical records. It has its own methodology and sample and has no equivalent in the Health Map Form.

section: ⚠ READ THIS FIRST: how to read the “Comparison” column
text:
⚠ READ THIS FIRST: how to read the “Comparison” column
This is the third of four documents. The first gave the overview, the second dealt with question design, this one maps coverage item by item, and the fourth points to ways of integrating and improving.
The six categories in the "Comparison" column:

Full overlap — both capture the same information, at equivalent depth.
Partial overlap (HHFA more complete) — the topic is covered by both, and the HHFA goes deeper.
Partial overlap (Health Map more complete) — the topic is covered by both, and the Health Map Form goes deeper.
Partial overlap (each captures a different aspect) — both deal with the same topic from different angles, and neither contains the other.
Minimal overlap (HHFA goes deeper) — the Health Map Form records the existence of the service in a single box, with no breakdown in the data, while the HHFA unfolds the same item into several verified elements. The laboratory is the case in point: the Form records "1. Laboratory: yes or no", while the HHFA asks which tests are done, with what equipment, with what reagents and under what quality control.
Minimal overlap (Health Map goes deeper) — the reverse: the HHFA has a single existence item and the Form unfolds it.
No overlap (HHFA only)
No overlap (Health Map only)

Why "minimal" is separated from "partial". The criterion is what is recorded, not what is defined. The Filling Guide defines several of these services precisely — for the laboratory, for instance, it requires thick smear, haemoglobin or haematocrit, and simple stool and urine analyses — but the Form has a single box for all four. Two facilities meeting different parts of the definition end up with the same tick. Calling this "partial" would be unfair to the items where the Form genuinely does unfold the topic, such as beds or devices.
The ◆ sign marks the difference in verification. Wherever it appears, the HHFA distinguishes within the answer itself what was observed from what was reported and not seen, whereas the Health Map Form has a single box to tick. Verification does take place in the field — the Health Map team is first informed and then confirms — but it is not recorded in the data. Two facilities with the same tick may be in different situations, and that difference disappears in the database.
The (add.) marker flags items that exist in the HHFA, but among the additional questions of the management and finance module. In an application using only the core questionnaires, they are not collected.
A note on method: the comparison is made at the level of the question, not of the published indicator. "Partial" refers to the depth of the information captured, not to the quality of the instrument: the two have different purposes, and each goes deeper in what it was designed for.

Two clarifications before the table, because this is the block where it is easiest to conclude that the two instruments ask the same thing.

Comment. On finance, it is worth being precise: the Health Map Form is not silent, but it approaches the topic through a single door — box 0.2 in the header, which records whether the facility has its own budget. Nothing further is asked about amounts, sources or fees. That is the exact definition of the “minimal” category, and it is also one of the points where adding three or four questions would have immediate effect on the public financial management work. As for the rest of the block, the difference is not one of topic, it is one of question. The Health Map Form maps the organizational chart: which directorates exist, which committees are constituted, which support services operate. The HHFA maps the activity: whether the board met in the past six months, whether the management committee uses the plan in its decisions, whether the facility received supervision, whether there is a budget and from what sources. Both readings are needed and neither replaces the other: without the chart one does not know whom to talk to; without the activity one does not know whether the chart corresponds to anything. title: 3  What each instrument captures about the reality of health facilities
text:
What this map shows
Full overlap is rare and concentrated in facility identification. Name, location, type, managing authority and a few support services. At those points, the two instruments produce directly comparable information.
Minimal overlap is the most frequent situation. In almost every support service, in almost every public health programme and in the budget, the Health Map Form records existence in a yes/no box and the HHFA unfolds the same item into several verified elements. The reason is always the same, and it was described in the second document: the service is recorded in a single tick, without its components, without readiness and without the distinction between what is reported and what is observed. It is also, for that reason, the group where additions yield most — unfolding one box into four costs little visit time.
Partial overlap comes next, and there the HHFA is usually the more complete, with clear exceptions for the building, the beds and the devices.
The specialty and the condition are not the same question. The Form names the specialty — endocrinology, cardiology, pulmonology — while the HHFA measures the capacity to manage diabetes, hypertension and asthma. For the hospital network the first counts; for primary health care the second does.
There is a clear set of items where it is the Health Map Form that captures more: the list of clinical and surgical specialties, the physical description of the building with areas and materials, general support services, the community extension of the service, and the fleet. These are the items that arise from the Health Map’s function as an instrument for network planning and for decisions on building works.
Complete absence of overlap concentrates on two opposite sides. On the HHFA side: workforce, noncommunicable diseases, infection prevention, essential medicines, financial management and clinical quality. On the Health Map side: everything to do with the building, the fleet and the physical link between facilities.

The apparent agility of the item question
The Health Map Form asks by item — “1. Laboratory”, “9. Endocrinology”, “1. Immunization”. That form has a real and immediate advantage: it fits on a page, it is filled in quickly, the enumerator never hesitates, and the facility answers without consulting anyone. This is why the item question is almost always the first choice of whoever designs a registration form, and it is the right choice when what one wants to know is which facilities exist and of what type.
What is worth anticipating is what happens next, when the data is used to decide. The item question has three consequences that only appear at the analysis stage, which is why it is often seen as more agile than it actually is.
First: the answer depends on who answers. “Do you have a laboratory?” is answered differently by a director thinking of the room, by a technician thinking of the tests he can run today, and by a manager thinking of what appears on the organizational chart. None of them is wrong — it is the question that admits all three readings. The Filling Guide resolves this on paper, by defining the required minimum, but the single box does not keep a record of which reading was used. The variation stays inside the data without being visible, and there is no way to correct for it in the analysis.
Second: the information drifts towards presence. In a list of items, the tick tends to be made when something of that kind exists. A facility doing thick smear and haemoglobin, but not the simple stool and urine analyses, is recorded as having a laboratory; a facility doing all four tests is recorded in exactly the same way. The resulting percentage is true, but it answers a weaker question than the one intended — and it tends to be read as though it answered the strong one.
Third, and most important: the item question does not close the decision, it postpones it. Knowing that a facility has an endocrinology consultation allows nothing to be decided about diabetes. The next question always comes: does it measure blood glucose? does it have metformin? does it have insulin and can it keep it cold? does it have staff trained in diagnosis and treatment? does it follow patients up, or see them once? Those questions will have to be asked anyway, later, in an additional survey — and an additional survey means another visit, another team and another budget. The item question is fast to collect and expensive to decide with.
This is why the HHFA replaces “do you have an endocrinology service?” with “does the facility diagnose, treat, follow up and counsel people with diabetes, and does it have the twelve items needed to do so?”. It is not a more demanding question for the sake of being demanding: it is the question the decision needs, asked once, in the same visit.


Why the HHFA is more complex
It is worth saying plainly where that complexity comes from, because it is neither arbitrary nor decorative. Seven design decisions explain almost all of it, and every one of them has appeared in the course of this document.

It measures installed capacity, not only existence. Every service the facility reports offering opens a set of questions on guidelines, trained staff, equipment, diagnostics and medicines. In the terms of the primary health care measurement framework, the Form stops at inputs while the HHFA moves on to process capacity — what the facility is in a position to do, not only what it holds.
It separates the observed from the reported. Almost every readiness item is physically verified, and the answer keeps that difference instead of dissolving it into a single tick. It is the information the Health Map team already gathers in the field and that is currently lost in the record.
It unfolds the service into its functions. Diagnosing, treating, counselling, referring and following up are different questions, asked by age group whenever that changes clinical conduct. A service that diagnoses but does not treat is not the same service.
It fixes the reference period of each question. Today, past 7 days, past 3 months, past 2 years. Without a stated period there is no way to compare two facilities with each other, or the same facility at two moments.
It fixes the denominator of each indicator. Every table in the inventory states the universe it is computed over: all facilities, or only those offering that service. This is what prevents comparing percentages built on different bases, and it is also what forces collection to be designed backwards, from the indicators one wants to produce.
It is internationally comparable. The inventory’s indicators carry permanent identifiers and fixed definitions, which allows Angola to be compared with itself over time and with other countries. That comparability has a price, and the price is standardization of the questions and the lists.
It is modular, so the complexity is chosen rather than imposed. Modules, core questions and additional questions allow the depth to be decided item by item. Nothing requires applying the whole instrument.

Put another way: the HHFA is longer because it answers, within the same visit, the questions the item question leaves open for later. Recognizing this takes nothing away from the Health Map Form, which answers very well what it was made to answer. It allows one to choose, item by item, where it is worth paying the cost of a more precise question and where the single box already says all that needs to be known. That is the work of the fourth document.

title: 4  How we can enhance the Health Map Form using the HHFA
text:
⚠ READ FIRST: the logic of this catalogue
The HHFA is not organised around questions. It is organised around indicators. The questions exist because there is an indicator that needs them, not the other way round. This catalogue follows the same order, and that is what distinguishes it from a list of questions to add.
Each proposal starts from an HHFA indicator and answers three questions: is that indicator already latent in the Form? If it is, what is missing from the question and the response options for it to be calculable? If it is not, what does it cost to bring it in?
Every addition is described by the same six fields:
This catalogue is not a form. It does not propose a closed version of the Form, nor a package to be adopted as a block. It presents pieces that can be compared with one another, so that the assembly — what goes in, in what order and in which facilities — is a decision for GEPE, taken with the cost and the gain of each piece in full view.
A note on purpose. The Health Map Form answers well to what it was designed for, and nothing in this document proposes replacing it with something else. What is proposed is to make the recording of what the Health Map team already collects more precise, and to add, where it pays off, what allows the network to be read not only by what exists but by what is in a condition to function.

title: 4  How we can enhance the Health Map Form using the HHFA
section: Type 1 — Identify the indicators already present and reformat the questions that create them
text:
Type 1 — Identify the indicators already present and reformat the questions that create them
Seven additions. This is the cheapest group and the one with the greatest immediate return, and most of it does not depend on observation.

1.1 Water source
Indicator identified: 2.1.1.1.2, percentage of facilities with an improved water source. It is latent: the Form already asks about the water source, and classifying it as improved or not is a convention applied to the source category.
The Form today: item 6.1, five categories of main source — piped network, borehole or well, tanker truck, none, other — and secondary sources in 6.1.2. With five categories it is not possible to separate a protected well from an unprotected one, nor a protected spring from an unprotected one, and that is exactly where the line of “improved” falls.
How the HHFA captures it:

Q1210: the same question, with thirteen categories, classified as improved and unimproved.
Q1211: “Is water from this source available on the facility grounds? If yes: may I see the water available today?” Yes, observed inside the building / Yes, observed on the grounds / Yes, reported and not seen / No, or only outside the grounds.

The HHFA indicator that becomes available: 2.1.1.1.2 = source in one of the improved categories and Q1211 other than 3 and 4.
Cost and mode: rewrite the categories of 6.1, from five to thirteen, plus one new box. Q1210 is self-reported; Q1211 is the point of observation. In self-reported mode the indicator can still be produced, but with category 3 indistinguishable from 1 and 2 — and the difference is on record, which is what matters.
What is gained. Improved water, present on the day, is a condition for any safe clinical act: hand hygiene, delivery care, instrument reprocessing. Distinguishing a protected well from an unprotected one changes how waterborne disease risk reads in a facility that treats sick people. For planning, the list of facilities where the source is unimproved — or where water exists but does not reach the grounds — is directly a list of interventions in boreholes, tanks and piping, which can be ranked by patient volume.


1.2 Energy source
Indicator identified: 2.1.1.1.1, percentage of facilities with electricity. Latent: the Form asks about the main source and the back-up source.
The Form today: item 6.2, four categories of main source and secondary sources in 6.2.2. There is nothing about functioning, and it is functioning that defines the indicator.
How the HHFA captures it:

Q1206: “Does this facility have electricity from any source — grid, generator, solar or other, including for stand-alone devices such as those of the EPI cold chain?” Yes / No.
Q1209: “During the last 7 days, was electricity, from the main or back-up source, available at all times when the facility was open?” Always, with no interruptions / Often, interruptions of less than 2 hours per day / Sometimes, frequent interruptions or interruptions of more than 2 hours per day.

The HHFA indicator that becomes available: 2.1.1.1.1 = Q1206==1 AND (Q1209==1 OR Q1209==2).
Cost and mode: one new box. Entirely self-reported.
Note. The indicator does not define “having electricity” as having a source: it defines it as having a source and less than two hours of outage per day. It is the same reality the Form already records, with a declared threshold — and it is that threshold that makes the number comparable across provinces and across years.
What is gained. Continuity of electricity underpins three things that decide outcomes: the vaccine cold chain, delivery care at night and the functioning of oxygen concentrators. A facility with a broken-down generator and a facility with stable power look the same in the Health Map today. Separating them allows solar energy investment to be directed where the return is immediate and measurable — in vaccines preserved, deliveries attended with light, and oxygen available.


1.3 Sanitation
Indicator identified: 2.1.1.1.3, percentage of facilities with improved sanitation accessible to clients and staff.
The Form today: item 6.3, three categories — bathroom or flush toilet, latrine, and the third. Three categories do not distinguish a flush toilet connected to a sewer from a flush toilet draining to an open site, nor an improved latrine from an open pit latrine.
How the HHFA captures it — Q1306: “Is there a toilet on the grounds accessible to outpatient clients or to staff? If yes: of what type? May I see it? If there are several, consider the most modern one.” Eleven type categories.
The HHFA indicator that becomes available: 2.1.1.1.3 = Q1306 in one of four specific categories.
Cost and mode: rewriting the categories only, zero new boxes. Self-reported is sufficient.
What is gained. Sanitation accessible to clients and staff weighs on the prevention of healthcare-associated infection and on service uptake, particularly by women and by people with reduced mobility. With the correct category, a facility with an open pit latrine is no longer counted alongside one with a toilet connected to a septic tank, and the list of sanitation rehabilitations comes straight out of the registry itself.


1.4 Communication
Indicators identified: 2.1.1.1.5 (communication system) and 2.1.1.1.6 (computer with internet).
The Form today: item 7.5.7, a single 0-1 box. It does not separate the facility’s telephone from the personal telephone of someone who works there, which is the distinction the indicator depends on.
How the HHFA captures it:

Q1201: “Does the facility have a means of communication with the outside — telephone or radio — supported by the facility?” Yes, functioning / Yes, broken down / No, only private telephones / No communication with the outside.
Q1202: functioning computer? · Q1203: access to e-mail or internet today? · Q1205: is the connection time paid for or reimbursed by management?

The HHFA indicators that become available: 2.1.1.1.5 = Q1201==1; 2.1.1.1.6 = Q1202==1 & Q1203==1 & Q1205==1.
Cost and mode: three new boxes. Self-reported.
What is gained. The facility’s means of communication — and not the personal mobile phone of someone who works there — is what sustains emergency referral, notification of diseases under mandatory reporting, and the sending of the monthly statistical report. The distinction reveals the facilities where the referral system and epidemiological surveillance depend on a staff member’s own pocket, which is a concrete and correctable vulnerability.


1.5 Emergency transport
Indicator identified: 2.1.1.1.7, percentage of facilities with an emergency transport system for patients.
The Form today: the transport service in 7.5.1 and the vehicle fleet counted in 10.1. The Form knows how many vehicles exist and whether they are functioning, but not whether one is available for an emergency today, with fuel and a driver — nor does it record the common case of a facility that has no vehicle of its own but can call one.
How the HHFA captures it:

Q1232: “Does the facility have access to a functioning ambulance or other vehicle for emergency transport of clients, stationed at this facility or one the facility can call?” Yes, ambulance / Yes, other type of vehicle / No.
Q1234: “Is the vehicle available, in working condition, with fuel and with a driver, today?”

The HHFA indicator that becomes available: 2.1.1.1.7 = (Q1232==1 OR Q1232==2) AND Q1234==1.
Cost and mode: two new boxes. Self-reported — the HHFA itself instructs the enumerator to ask someone who knows, not to go and look.
What is gained. This is the indicator that bears most directly on maternal and neonatal mortality, because it measures the existence of a route of evacuation today, and not the existence of a vehicle in the inventory. Combined with the distance to the referral facility that the Form already records in 3.2 — in minutes and in kilometres of tarred road and dirt track — it allows identification of the areas where obstetric evacuation is not feasible within a useful time window. It is one of the most valuable readings the two instruments together can produce.


1.6 Waste treatment
Indicators identified: 2.5.1.1.12 and 2.5.1.1.13, safe final disposal of sharps waste and of non-sharps infectious waste.
The Form today: items 6.5 and 6.6, treatment of general and medical waste. The topic is covered; what is missing is the category of final disposal and verification that the treatment method works.
How the HHFA captures it: Q1214 to Q1220 — final disposal with eleven categories, observation of the site, and two questions that decide the indicator: is the incinerator working today, and does it have fuel.
The HHFA indicators that become available: 2.5.1.1.12 and 2.5.1.1.13, both requiring adequate final disposal and Q1219==1 AND Q1220==1.
Cost and mode: rewrite the categories of 6.5 and 6.6, plus two boxes. The categories work self-reported; the two questions about the incinerator require observation.
What is gained. Final waste disposal protects three groups at once: the staff who handle it, the clients and the community around the facility. The question of whether the incinerator is lit and has fuel turns an infrastructure datum into a maintenance list — almost always a cheap one — that today no one can extract from the Health Map.


1.7 Equipment
Indicators identified: table 2.2.1.1, basic equipment of the main service area. Four of the Form’s items correspond directly to indicators: adult scale (2.2.1.1.8), sphygmomanometer (2.2.1.1.3), clinical stethoscope (2.2.1.1.2) and infant scale (2.2.1.1.10).
The Form today: item 9.1, a count of fifteen types of equipment “usually in working order”, for health centres and health posts. The count answers a logistics question — how many devices exist in the network — not the indicator’s question, which is what proportion of facilities have the device available and functioning on the day of the visit.
How the HHFA captures it — Q1322, a grid with two columns: “For each item I ask about, show me the item and tell me, where applicable, whether it is functioning.”


available: observed / reported, not seen / no


functional: yes / no / does not know


The HHFA indicators that become available: one per item, in the format Q1322_nA==1 & Q1322_nB==1, with a denominator of all facilities.
Cost and mode: two boxes per row. Requires observation — column B does not survive self-completion.
Design note. The Form’s count should not be replaced by the grid. The two pieces of information serve different decisions, and the recommendation is to keep them side by side: the count for equipment distribution, the functioning column to know where the failures are.
What is gained. The scale, the sphygmomanometer and the stethoscope are the minimum needed to monitor a pregnancy, detect hypertension and follow up a malnourished child — without them, the consultation takes place without measurement. The count says how many devices exist in the network; the functioning column says in which facilities care is compromised today. The difference between the two numbers is the size of the maintenance problem, which at present is visible nowhere and which is usually cheaper to solve than buying new equipment.

Type 1 summary. Seven additions, around twelve new boxes and the rewriting of the categories of four items. Five of the HHFA’s seven basic amenities indicators become calculable without any additional visit. This is the group to consider first, because it improves the Form without altering the collection process.

section: Type 2 — Indicators latent in the Filling Guide’s definition
text:
Type 2 — Indicators latent in the Filling Guide’s definition
This group has a property worth making explicit: the Form is not being asked to start asking about something else, it is being asked to record what it has already decided to ask. The Filling Guide defines several services precisely; the Form resolves each definition into a single tick, and the components are lost.

2.1 Laboratory
Indicators identified: table 2.3.1.1, basic diagnostic capacity — in particular 2.3.1.1.1 (haemoglobin on site) and 2.3.1.1.8 (malaria diagnosis on site).
The Form today: item 7.2.1, a single box. To tick it, the Guide requires that at least thick blood smear, haemoglobin or haematocrit, and simple stool and urine tests be performed. The definition contains the indicators; the single tick loses them, because a facility that performs two of the four is recorded exactly like one that performs all four.
How the HHFA captures it: grids of tests available at the point of care itself, test by test, with verification that the reagent is within its validity date and that the items needed to run the test are available and functioning.
The HHFA indicators that become available: one per test, in the format 2.3.1.1.x, with a denominator of all facilities.
Cost and mode: four boxes where today there is one, if one keeps to the Guide’s definition. The HHFA calculation rule counts the test only if the reagent is within its validity date, so the complete indicator requires observation. In self-reported mode the unpacking is still worthwhile — it separates those who perform two tests from those who perform four — but it produces a declared version of the indicator, and that should be written into the documentation so that there is no confusion in the analysis.
What is gained. The four tests the Guide already requires are not an arbitrary list: the thick blood smear underpins malaria diagnosis, haemoglobin detects anaemia in pregnant women and children, and urinalysis is the screening test for pre-eclampsia and urinary infection in pregnancy. Knowing which of them each facility performs makes two things possible that are not possible today: directing reagents and training to the concrete gaps, and estimating in which part of the network malaria treatment is being given without laboratory confirmation — information that is central for the national programme.


2.2 Deliveries
Indicators identified: the signal functions of emergency obstetric care, 3.1.3.2.1 to 3.1.3.2.7, and the composite indicators 3.1.3.1.3 (basic emergency obstetric care) and its equivalent for comprehensive care.
The Form today: items 7.3.7.1 and 7.3.7.2, two boxes, BEmONC and CEmONC. The Guide defines BEmONC as “Antibiotics, Oxytocin and parenteral Anticonvulsant, manual removal of the placenta and of retained products” — five of the seven international signal functions, already written down — and CEmONC as “All of B plus surgery (caesarean sections and blood transfusion)”. Two functions are missing from the definition: assisted vaginal delivery and neonatal resuscitation.
How the HHFA captures it: each signal function is a question, with the reference period stated.
The HHFA indicators that become available: one per signal function, plus the composite indicators — which become calculated from their components instead of being declared by the respondent. This is an important change: today, ticking BEmONC is a judgement made by whoever fills in the Form; with the components separated, it becomes a result.
Cost and mode: nine boxes where today there are two. Works self-reported, because the question is about what the facility performs, not about an object to be observed.
Note. This addition aligns the Form with the international standard for emergency obstetric care and gives any EmONC assessment under way a far better sampling base than it would otherwise have.
What is gained. The signal functions are the internationally accepted measure of a facility’s capacity to save a woman with haemorrhage, with eclampsia or in obstructed labour, and to resuscitate a newborn who is not breathing. The practical gain lies in granularity: today we know that a facility does not have basic emergency obstetric care, but we do not know which of the five functions it lacks. With the components separated we come to know — and in most cases only one is missing, frequently because of the absence of a medicine or of a short training course. It is one of the highest-impact interventions per unit of cost in the whole network.


2.3 Other unpackings of definitions
The same reasoning applies to four further items where the Guide is already precise and the Form keeps a single tick.

7.3.6 Antenatal care
Twelve components: card, history, weight, oedema, fundal height, mucous membranes, blood pressure, Leopold’s manoeuvres, intermittent preventive treatment of malaria, iron and folic acid, deworming, counselling
3.1.2.1.x, antenatal care components, one by one
Distinguishes complete antenatal care from antenatal care of registration only, and identifies which component is missing in each facility — the basis of any maternal health improvement plan


7.3.9 Family planning
At least one modern method — injectable, pill, IUD, diaphragm — excluding the condom
3.1.1.1.x, provision by method
Shows the real breadth of choice offered to the woman, which is what determines method uptake and continuation

Makes it possible to link growth monitoring to early detection of malnutrition, instead of addressing it only once it is severe

Reveals where the emergency service is an open door and where it is an emergency service with means — a decisive distinction for the design of the referral network



All of them work in self-reported mode.

Type 2 summary. Six additions. The gain is disproportionate to the cost, because it converts ticks that depend on the judgement of whoever fills in the Form into verifiable facts, and almost all of it works in self-reported mode. It is also the group that is easiest to justify to the facilities, because nothing new is being asked of them.

title: 4  How we can enhance the Health Map Form using the HHFA
section: Type 3 — Readiness indicators, with the denominator already guaranteed
text:
Type 3 — Readiness indicators, with the denominator already guaranteed

The central argument of this catalogue is here. The HHFA readiness indicators have a restricted denominator: they are calculated among the facilities that offer the service. The Health Map Form already produces that denominator — it is exactly what the boxes in section 7.3 do, service by service, in every facility in the country.
What is missing is not the denominator. It is the numerator. And the numerator, in its minimal form, is three identical questions for every service.


3.1 The readiness trio
Since they are always the same three questions, enumerator training is short and the data structure is regular.
Guidelines available — how the HHFA captures it, in the case of antenatal care, Q1817: “For each document I ask about, please show it to me.” Observed / Reported, not seen / Not available.
Trained staff — Q1818: “In the last 2 years, have you or any antenatal care provider received training in any of the following topics?” Yes / No.
Tracer medicine or commodity — one item per service, with the validity scale described in Type 4.


3.2 Antenatal care, as a fully worked example
Indicators identified: 3.1.2.2.1 (antenatal care guidelines available) and 3.1.2.2.5 (staff trained in antenatal care), among the 46 indicators of the sub-area.
The Form today: box 7.3.6 records that the facility provides antenatal care. That box is, without the Form having intended it, the exact filter for the HHFA’s antenatal care readiness indicators.
The HHFA indicators that become available: 3.1.2.2.1 = Q1817_1==1 OR Q1817_2==1, among facilities offering the service; 3.1.2.2.5 = Q1818_1==1, with the same denominator.
Cost and mode: two boxes per service, three if the tracer is included. Training works self-reported; guidelines only produce the HHFA indicator with observation.
What is gained. Availability of guidelines on site and recent training of the person delivering the care are two of the factors most consistently associated with the quality of antenatal care. The gain is moving from “antenatal care exists” to “antenatal care exists, the person providing it was trained in the last two years and has the guideline to hand” — which is exactly the question a national training plan needs to answer in order to know where to invest. Multiplied across the chosen services, this trio is what turns the Health Map from an inventory of the network into an instrument for quality planning.

It is also the one where the Health Map’s earlier investment pays off most, because it makes use of a national denominator that already exists.

section: Type 4 — Indicators that require a new block
text:
Type 4 — Indicators that require a new block
No latency in the Form. The discussion becomes one of priority and cost. They are presented in increasing order of effort.

4.1 Staffing establishment and workforce
Indicators identified: 1.2.1.1.1, percentage of facilities with an approved staffing establishment with numbers assigned by qualification; and table 1.2.1, the count of professionals by category.
The Form today: nothing. The Form records who runs the facility — general, clinical and pedagogical management, heads of unit — but not how many people work there nor in which categories.
How the HHFA captures it — Q301: “Does this facility have a staffing establishment, with authorised numbers by qualification?” Yes / No — followed by the count by professional category.
The HHFA indicators that become available: 1.2.1.1.1 = Q301==1, and the count indicators of sub-area 1.2.1.
Cost and mode: one box for the indicator above, plus one line per professional category. Entirely self-reported — it comes from the facility’s own staffing records and requires no physical verification.
Note, and it is the most important one in this catalogue. The Form already collects the catchment population (item 3.1). With the staff count, HHFA sub-area 1.2.2 — densities of professionals per 10,000 population — becomes calculable from two fields that sit on the same form. It is the only point in the whole catalogue where a cheap, self-reported addition produces system-level indicators, and not only facility-level ones.
It is the cheapest new block and the one that closes the largest asymmetry identified in document 3.
What is gained. The density of professionals per 10,000 population is the indicator that underpins any decision on staff allocation and recruitment, and it is what Angola needs to report under international commitments on human resources for health. The greater gain, however, is internal: the provincial count conceals the distribution within the province, and it is within the province that the inequalities lie that can be corrected by transfer. Knowing which facilities do not have a single professional of a given category is, in itself, a management decision.


4.2 Essential medicines, and the anchors the Form already has
Indicators identified: table 2.4.1.1, one indicator per medicine.
The Form today: item 7.2.10 records “Pharmacy — exists, functioning”. It is a question about the service: there is a place, with someone responsible, that dispenses medicines. Nothing is said about what is inside it, and no indicator from table 2.4.1.1 can be obtained from it.
But there are four points in the Form where a specific medicine is already asked about, without the Form treating it as such: the distribution of vitamin A (7.3.2), the distribution of albendazole (7.3.3), oral rehydration (7.3.4.1) and the therapeutic nutrition centre (7.3.4.2) — this last one because the Guide defines the service by the therapeutic food it dispenses. In those four cases, ticking the box already implies asserting that the product is available.
They are called anchors because they are the natural place to start. Making the item explicit at those four points introduces no new topic, it only writes down what the question already presupposes — it is, in practice, a Type 2 addition inside a Type 4 block. A list of forty medicines is another conversation, and it is fair that it be discussed as such.
How the HHFA captures it — the Q3102 scale, which is the best-designed one in the instrument: “For each medicine I ask about, show it to me. Check that at least one unit of the type is not expired.”

At least one within the validity date
Available, but expired
Reported available, not seen
Not available today
Never available

The indicators count code 1 only. The distinction between 1, 2 and 3 is exactly the difference between the facility having metformin and the facility being able to give metformin to someone today.
Cost and mode: one box per medicine. Observation only — under self-completion the scale loses all meaning, because all the information lies in the distinction between the first three categories.
Methodological caveat, to be recorded in the documentation. Several indicators in table 2.4.1.1 count the medicine if it is seen in the pharmacy or in the delivery room or in the emergency trolley. A collection that looks only at the pharmacy underestimates those items — oxytocin, magnesium sulfate, chlorhexidine, adrenaline, dexamethasone and morphine. That is not a reason not to collect; it is a reason to state the restriction alongside the number.
What is gained. The effective availability of the medicine on the day is the most direct determinant of whether the patient leaves the consultation with treatment. Separating has it, from has it but expired, from says it has it and does not show it, identifies stock management failures that no requisition system can reveal — because the requisition system records what was sent, not what is on the shelf. Starting with the four anchors, the gain is immediate and cheap: it becomes possible to know whether vitamin A, albendazole, oral rehydration salts and therapeutic food are actually available in the facilities that declare they offer those services.


4.3 Standard precautions and infection prevention
Indicators identified: table 2.5.1.1.
The Form today: absent, with two important exceptions — items 6.5 and 6.6 already cover waste treatment (see 1.6), and sterilisation is recorded in 7.2.14.
How the HHFA captures it — Q1320, a grid of seventeen rows with a three-level scale: “For each item I ask about, show me the item.” Observed / Reported, not seen / Not available. It includes clean running water, soap, alcohol-based hand rub, disposable gloves, single-use syringes, sharps and non-sharps waste containers, and environmental disinfectant.
The HHFA indicators that become available: hand hygiene (2.5.1.1.5), gloves (2.5.1.1.6), syringes (2.5.1.1.7), disinfectant (2.5.1.1.9), sharps waste storage (2.5.1.1.10) and non-sharps waste storage (2.5.1.1.11) — six indicators from a single grid. Two stand-alone questions add waste management guidelines (2.5.1.1.2) and trained staff (2.5.1.1.4).
Cost and mode: around twenty boxes. Requires observation.
What is gained. Infection prevention protects patients and health workers at the same time, and it is the foundation on which any patient safety programme rests. What makes this block attractive is the nature of the items: soap, alcohol-based hand rub, gloves, a sharps box and disinfectant are cheap products, locally procurable, whose absence has disproportionate consequences. It is one of the few domains where measuring leads almost automatically to a correction that is feasible in the short term.


4.4 Chronic conditions
Indicators identified: 3.3.1 (cardiovascular diseases, 46 indicators), 3.3.2 (diabetes, 26) and 3.3.3 (chronic respiratory disease, 26).
The Form today: the hospital specialty boxes — cardiology (7.1.7), endocrinology (7.1.9), pulmonology (7.1.25) — record how the facility is organised, not the capacity to manage the condition. As described in document 3, these are different questions: the specialty says how the facility is organised, the condition says what the facility is able to resolve. In primary health care, where hypertension, diabetes and asthma are managed without a specialist, it is the second that decides.
How the HHFA captures it: for each condition, provision broken down by function — diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, self-care counselling — followed by the readiness trio and the tracer items.
The HHFA indicators that become available: provision by function works self-reported and is cheap: four boxes per condition. The tracer items require observation.
Cost and mode: it is proposed to start with provision by function, in three conditions, twelve boxes, self-reported mode. The tracers come in with the medicines block, if that one moves forward.
What is gained. Hypertension and diabetes represent a growing burden of disease, above all in urban areas, and they are conditions that can be managed at the primary level — provided the facility diagnoses, treats and follows up. Measuring capacity by condition and not by specialty is precisely what allows the decentralisation of chronic disease management to health centres and health posts to be planned, which is one of the structuring decisions of the primary health care reform. Without this data, that decentralisation is planned blind.


4.5 Other blocks to consider









Block
HHFA indicators
Cost and mode
What is gained




Malaria, diagnosis and treatment
3.2.2.1.1 to 3.2.2.1.8 — the Form records the distribution of mosquito nets, but not the malaria service
8 boxes, self-reported for provision
Gives the national programme a map of diagnostic and treatment capacity for the country’s leading cause of demand for care

1 box per tracer, self-reported, comes from the pharmacy records
Separates a one-off failure from a structural supply failure — the first is solved at the facility, the second in the logistics chain


Accessibility for people with reduced mobility
1.1.3.1.1 to 1.1.3.1.5 — ramps, handrails, accessible toilet
5 boxes, observation
Makes access measurable for older people, people with disabilities and wheelchair users, today invisible in the planning of building works


Budget and sources of financing
4.2.1.1.1, autonomy to manage its own bank account, and following. The Form has item 0.2, a box on having its own budget — that is the natural anchor
6 to 8 boxes, self-reported
Links the Health Map to the work on modernising public financial management in health, giving it for the first time a facility-level basis

Shows which part of the network is effectively covered by municipal and provincial supervision, which is the main existing mechanism for continuous improvement




Type 4 summary. Ten blocks. It is not proposed to adopt them together. Two of them — the staffing establishment and provision by function for chronic conditions — are self-reported, cheap and of great return, and can be considered alongside Types 1 and 2. The remainder require observation and should be decided in light of the collection mode the Health Map comes to adopt.

title: 4  How we can enhance the Health Map Form using the HHFA
text:
How to read this catalogue
The additions do not add up in a single order. They can be grouped by type, by mode of collection, by thematic area or by the facilities they apply to. Three readings seem useful:
By latency. Types 1 and 2 make calculable indicators that the Form already pursues without producing them. They introduce no new topics and, for the most part, require no visit. This is the reading that costs least to defend to the facilities and the one that changes the current process least.
By mode of collection. There is a set of additions — Types 1 and 2 almost in their entirety, the staffing establishment, provision by function for chronic conditions, stock-outs, the budget — that works in self-reported mode and can enter an edition of the Form without changing anything in the collection. And there is another set that only makes sense where there is an enumerator and observation. This separation allows the two to move at different speeds.
By denominator. Type 3 is the one that best uses what already exists. Over four editions, the Health Map has built a national denominator service by service — the information on which facilities offer what. That denominator is precisely what the HHFA readiness indicators require and what a sample survey cannot produce with the same coverage. Three questions per service turn it into measured readiness.
By the gain. This is the reading that best serves a discussion with the national programmes, because it is the one that speaks their language. Grouped by what they produce, the additions concentrate in four areas: maternal and newborn health — delivery signal functions, antenatal care components, emergency transport, haemoglobin and urinalysis; child health and nutrition — child health monitoring, vitamin A, therapeutic food, functioning scales, a cold chain sustained by continuous electricity; chronic diseases — capacity by condition instead of by specialty; and patient and health worker safety — standard precautions, waste, water and sterilisation. Each programme recognises in this list what it needs, and that makes the adoption of the additions a shared conversation rather than an external requirement.
What remains to be decided is not technical. It is a matter of knowing which indicators Angola wants to produce, about which facilities, and at what frequency. That is the subject of the next document.
